title: Thermal Expansion of Solids

notes.heading: 1. Linear (α), Superficial (β) & Volume (γ) Expansion
notes.proseLatex: Heating an isotropic solid by $\Delta T$ expands every linear dimension — including cavities and hole diameters! — according to $L = L_0(1 + \alpha\Delta T)$, area $A = A_0(1 + \beta\Delta T)$, and volume $V = V_0(1 + \gamma\Delta T)$. For small $\alpha\Delta T \ll 1$, isotropic solids satisfy the exact ratio $\alpha : \beta : \gamma = 1 : 2 : 3$, while solid density decreases with temperature as $\rho_T = \frac{\rho_0}{1 + \gamma\Delta T} \approx \rho_0(1 - \gamma\Delta T)$.

keyFormulas.label: Isotropic Expansion Coefficients & Density Shift
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Relate alpha, beta, gamma and compute heated density or cavity expansion.

examples.problemLatex: If the linear expansion coefficient of brass is $\alpha = 1.9\times 10^{-5}\text{ }^\circ\text{C}^{-1}$, find the percentage increase in volume of a brass sphere heated by $100^\circ\text{C}$.

notes.heading: 2. Bimetallic Strips, Constant-Difference Rods & Pendulum Clock Drift
notes.proseLatex: When two welded strips ($\alpha_1 > \alpha_2$) are heated, the bimetallic strip bends with the HIGHER-$\alpha$ metal on the OUTER convex side (and flips concave on cooling). Two rods maintain a temperature-independent length difference $L_2 - L_1 = \text{const}$ if and only if $L_1\alpha_1 = L_2\alpha_2$. A metal pendulum clock ($T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$) lengthens when heated, increasing $T$ so the clock runs SLOW and loses $\frac{\Delta t}{t} = \frac{1}{2}\alpha\Delta T$ seconds per second.

keyFormulas.label: Constant Length Difference & Pendulum Clock Loss
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Design temperature-compensated rods and compute seconds lost/gained per day.

notes.heading: 3. Real vs Apparent Liquid Expansion & Anomalous Water (4 °C)
notes.proseLatex: Because a heated container also expands ($\gamma_g = 3\alpha_g$), observed apparent expansion of a liquid $\gamma_{\text{app}}$ is smaller than real expansion $\gamma_{\text{real}} = \gamma_{\text{app}} + \gamma_g$. Water exhibits anomalous behaviour between $0^\circ\text{C}$ and $4^\circ\text{C}$: heating from $0^\circ\text{C}$ to $4^\circ\text{C}$ CONTRACTS its volume, reaching MAXIMUM density ($1000\text{ kg/m}^3$) and MINIMUM volume at $4^\circ\text{C}$, allowing aquatic life to survive beneath $0^\circ\text{C}$ surface ice.

keyFormulas.label: Real vs Apparent Liquid Expansion
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Account for container expansion and water's 4 deg C density maximum.

wbjeebTraps: Photographic-enlargement rule: heating a metal plate with a circular hole INCREASES the hole's diameter (never shrinks inward!).
Heating water filled to the brim at $4^\circ\text{C}$ OR cooling it below $4^\circ\text{C}$ BOTH cause water to overflow, because volume is minimum at $4^\circ\text{C}$.
In pendulum drift $\Delta t/t = \frac{1}{2}\alpha\Delta\theta$, don't forget the factor $\frac{1}{2}$ from $\sqrt{L}$ nor $86{,}400\text{ s/day}$.
